title: Correlation vs. Causation: Directionality & Third Variables
description: Unpack why correlation does not imply causation: reverse directionality, confounding third variables, and spurious relationships.

slides.title: The Golden Rule of Science ⚠️
slides.content:
# Correlation Does Not Equal Causation

No phrase is repeated more often in research methods than: *'Correlation does not imply causation.'* Yet media headlines and everyday intuition routinely violate it. When variable A correlates with variable B, three distinct causal realities are possible:

1. **A causes B**: The presumed causal direction.
2. **B causes A (The Directionality Problem)**: The reverse causal direction is equally supported by the correlation.
3. **C causes both A and B (The Third-Variable Problem)**: An unmeasured third variable causes the apparent co-variation between A and B, creating a **spurious correlation**.

A correlation tells you that two things travel together; it cannot tell you which one drives the car!

quizData.question: A cross-sectional study discovers a strong positive correlation between low self-esteem and clinical depression. What is the directionality problem in interpreting this finding?

options.text: It is impossible to tell whether low self-esteem causes depression, or depression causes low self-esteem
Self-esteem cannot be measured using surveys
The correlation coefficient must be negative rather than positive
The sample size was too small to calculate p-values

quizData.explanation: Because both variables were measured at the same single point in time, temporal precedence is unknown: low self-esteem could cause depression, or depression could degrade self-esteem.

slides.title: The Third-Variable Problem & Spurious Correlations 🍦
slides.content:
## Ice Cream and Drowning Deaths

Consider this empirical fact: In coastal cities, monthly ice cream sales correlate strongly and positively with monthly swimming pool drownings (r = +0.85). Does eating ice cream cause people to drown? Does drowning make people crave ice cream?

* The true causal agent is **Outdoor Temperature (Variable C)**.
* In hot summer months, heat causes more people to buy ice cream AND causes more people to go swimming, naturally increasing drownings.
* When you statistically control for temperature (calculating a **partial correlation**), the correlation between ice cream and drowning drops to zero!

Whenever a third variable creates an illusory causal relationship between two unrelated variables, it is called a **spurious correlation**.

quizData.question: A study finds that children who sleep with a nightlight on have significantly higher rates of myopia (nearsightedness) in teenage years. What third variable accounted for this spurious correlation?

options.text: Parental myopia (nearsighted parents need nightlights to see and pass on genetic myopia)
The color of the bedroom wall paint

quizData.explanation: Myopic parents were more likely to put nightlights in their children's rooms, and they genetically transmitted myopia to their offspring; the nightlight itself was harmless.

slides.title: Psychology Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
### Cross-Lagged Panel Designs

How can correlational researchers combat the directionality problem without a true experiment? Use a **cross-lagged longitudinal design**! Measure both Variable A and Variable B at Time 1, and measure both again at Time 2. If Time 1 A correlates with Time 2 B stronger than Time 1 B correlates with Time 2 A, you establish **temporal precedence**—a key requirement of causality!
